entities.summary:
Antipope Felix II was installed as Pope in 355 AD after Emperor Constantius II banished the reigning Pope, Liberius, for refusing to subscribe to a sentence of condemnation against Saint Athanasius. This event was a significant moment in the struggle between the orthodox and Arian factions within the Roman Empire. Felix II's papacy was short-lived, lasting only until his death on November 22, 365 AD. Despite his brief tenure, Felix II's actions had a lasting impact on the development of the Christian Church in Rome.

Felix II was previously an Archdeacon of Rome and had played a key role in the Roman See's relations with the Eastern Roman Empire. His appointment as Pope was seen as a victory for the Arian faction, which had been gaining momentum in the empire. However, Felix II's papacy was marked by controversy and opposition, including a bitter dispute with the Emperor Constantius II over the appointment of a new Patriarch of Alexandria.

The legacy of Antipope Felix II can be seen in the ongoing struggle between the orthodox and Arian factions within the Christian Church. His actions also had significant repercussions for the Roman Empire, contributing to a period of instability and power struggles that would shape the course of imperial history. As the leader of the Arian faction, Felix II played a key role in the development of the Eastern Roman Empire's relations with the Western Roman Empire, setting the stage for a century of conflict and competition between the two powers.

In the years following his death, Felix II's reputation would be remembered as one of the most tumultuous and divisive figures in the history of the Roman See. His legacy would be marked by controversy and division, but also by a deep commitment to the principles of the Arian faction and the interests of the Eastern Roman Empire.
